items.title: Twenty in two minutes
items.prose: A fresh block of 20 in the 80-in-8 mix, four options each. Target: 2 minutes, 6 s a question. Time yourself with your own watch; the page has no clock. Count your amber rows on the first Check.
items.question: Type the letter of each answer.

feedback.correct: All twenty right. Compare your time and amber count with your block from the lesson.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Note the amber rows by kind, then redo them.

explain.text: Each row needed one move from the course. Compare your time with the lesson block. If one kind was amber twice, it is your drill this week.

items.title: Ten sequences, ten word problems
items.prose: Ten sequences at 8 seconds each, then ten word problems at 10 seconds each: 3 minutes in all. Time yourself with your own watch. Times as HH:MM; a loss or a fall with a minus sign.
items.question: Fill in all twenty.

rows: An order of 6,000 shares is 15% filled: shares filled
Leave 13:52; the journey takes 3 h 24 min: arrive at
£2,000 at 6% simple interest for 3 months: interest (£)
A share falls 20%, then rises 20%: net change (%)

feedback.correct: All twenty right. Compare your time with the 3-minute target.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Redo the amber rows: differences first, or the one line first.

byKey.r4c1: Each term adds the two before: $7 + 11 = 18$.
byKey.r5c1: Gaps 3, 5, 7, 9: next 11, so 35. These are the squares less 1.

explain.text: The sequences fell to differences, ratios, lists or weaving, in that order of speed. The word problems were one line each, with unit changes in rows 13, 14, 16 and 19. Time the slower half again tomorrow.

items.title: Generate your own mock
items.prose:
`mock_generator(seed, mix)` returns a list of `(text, options, answer)` tuples, `mix[kind]` of each kind, from `random.Random(seed)`. Options are four different positive numbers, the answer among them once, each wrong one within a factor of ten of it. Text formats:

| Kind | Text |
|---|---|
| `addsub` | `291 + 883`, `508 − 96` |
| `mul`, `div` | `41 × 63`, `342 ÷ 6` (a whole answer) |
| `dec` | `8.3 × 8`, `34.8 ÷ 1.2` |
| `frac` | `2/3 − 1/2` (answers as `Fraction`) |
| `pct` | `15% of 1,260` |
| `seq` | `66, 57, 48, 39, ?` |

Sequences need fixed gaps, fixed second gaps, or each term $r$ times the last plus $c$.
items.question: Write `mock_generator(seed, mix)`.

widget.how: Check runs 14 hidden tests. A hidden reader parses each text and recomputes the answer with fractions, counts the kinds against the mix, checks four distinct options with the answer once and every option within ten times the answer, whole division answers, and that one seed gives one paper and another seed another.

feedback.correct: Your generator makes papers whose answers recompute, whose kinds match the mix, and whose wrong options are near misses.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read which hidden test failed: the kind counts, a recomputed answer, the options, or the seed.

explain.text: Every random choice comes from one `random.Random(seed)`, so a seed fixes a paper and exam authors can rebuild it. Working in `Fraction` keeps 0.1 + 0.2 from ever deciding an answer. Near misses come from the slips this level named: a carry, a moved point, the reverse operation.

items.title: Differences, then ratios
items.prose: Extend `next_by_differences` from the lesson. `next_term(seq)` tries differences first; then a constant ratio; then a ratio with a fixed step, each term $k$ times the last plus $c$. It returns `None` if none fits. Work in `fractions.Fraction`, so 9, 6, 4 gives exactly $\tfrac83$.
items.question: Write `next_term(seq)`.

widget.starter:
from fractions import Fraction


def next_term(seq):
    t = [Fraction(x) for x in seq]
    answer = Fraction(0)
    # differences, then a ratio, then a ratio with a fixed step
    ...
    return answer
widget.how: Check runs 13 hidden tests, compared exactly: three by differences, four ratios (one of them $\tfrac83$ as a Fraction), two ratios with a step, and three that fit nothing and return None.

feedback.correct: Differences, then ratios, then a ratio with a step, all exact.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the lesson’s order, and use Fraction so no float rounds a ratio.

explain.text: Differences settle for fixed gaps and growing gaps; a doubling sequence never settles, so ratios come next. 3, 5, 9, 17, 33 needs the step: $k = 2$, $c = -1$. Fibonacci fits none of the three, which is why the lesson keeps known lists as a separate test.

items.title: The review, in order
items.prose: You have just sat a mock of 80 in 8. Put the review routine in order. Two lines are habits that waste the review: leave them out.
items.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: Score it net, +1 right and −1 wrong, so you know where you stand against the pass line
Mark each block’s time against 2, 4, 6 and 8 minutes, to see where the time went
List every wrong answer and every right answer over 12 s, with its seconds
Sort each into a slip, a method gap or a time loss, by its mark and seconds
Count the method gaps and time losses by kind, because slips need care rather than a drill
Pick one drill for the kind with the most, and book the next mock for a week later
Redo only the wrong answers until each one is right
lines.why: That skips the slow right answers, which cost questions too, and it rehearses these answers rather than the method.

lines.text: Drill every kind a little each day
lines.why: Spread over seven kinds, no weak kind improves. One drill, chosen by the count, does.

feedback.correct: Score, time, list, sort, count, then one drill and a date for the next mock.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Measure first, then sort, then choose.

byKey.d1: That skips the slow right answers, which cost questions too, and it rehearses these answers rather than the method.
byKey.d2: Spread over seven kinds, no weak kind improves. One drill, chosen by the count, does.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the two habits belongs.
byKey.o3: List the errors once the score and the times are down.
byKey.o4: Sort only after the list is made.
byKey.o6: Choosing the drill comes last, from the count.

explain.text: The score and the block times say how far off you are and where. The list and the sort say why. The count chooses one drill, and the next mock checks whether it worked.

items.prose: A forward-only test, four options, +1 right and −1 wrong; a question you never reach scores 0. With 30 s left, five questions remain. You can remove one wrong option from each, then guess.
items.question: What is the expected net score from guessing all five?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find one guess’s value among three, then times five.

byKey.blind: −2.5 is five blind guesses among four. You removed one option, so each is among three.
byKey.two-removed: 0 needs two options removed from each. With one removed, each guess costs a third.
byKey.one-guess: That is one guess. There are five.

explain.text: Each guess among three is worth $\tfrac13 - \tfrac23 = -\tfrac13$, so five are worth $-\tfrac53$. Leaving them unreached scores 0, so here guessing costs marks. Remove a second option, and each guess becomes free.

items.prose: A test has 60 questions in 10 minutes. At 4 minutes you finish question 20.
items.question: How many questions behind pace are you?

feedback.correct: 10 s a question puts pace at Q24: 4 behind.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find this test’s pace first.

byKey.used-six: You used 6 s, the 80-in-8 pace. Here it is $600 \div 60 = 10$ s.
byKey.sign: That says ahead. Pace is Q24 and you are at Q20.

explain.text: 600 s over 60 questions is 10 s each, so 240 s is Q24. You are at Q20, four behind, which is 40 s. Every test needs its own checkpoints.

items.title: The week before the test
items.prompt: Write your plan for the week before an 80-questions-in-8-minutes test. Include: (a) daily warm-up rounds and the scores you will track; (b) the drills you will do, chosen from an error review, with their target times; (c) when you will sit a mock and how you will review it; (d) your checkpoints; (e) your skip and guess rules for a test that allows skipping and for one that does not; (f) the first-minute rule; (g) what you will do after a bad start.
items.model:
**The plan for the week before an 80-in-8 test.**

**1. Warm-up every day.** Five rounds of the daily warm-up from Today, about 10 minutes. I note every score. This week my best is 41; the Stage 3 mark is 50. I aim for a best of 45 by Friday and a daily average that rises. A round at 50 is 2.4 s an answer, well inside the test’s 6 s.

**2. Drills from my last review.** My mock review found five fraction method gaps and three slow sequences. So each day:

- 20 fraction sums at 6 s each, 2 minutes, one denominator first;
- 12 sequences at 8 s each, 96 s, differences first.

Slips get care, not a drill: I check the decimal point and the last digit.

**3. One mock mid-week.** On Wednesday I sit a full mock of 80 against my own watch, then run the review: net score, block times, sort into slips, method gaps and time losses, count by kind. Thursday’s drill follows from that count.

**4. Checkpoints.** I write Q20 2:00, Q40 4:00, Q60 6:00 at the top of my paper before the test starts. Ten a minute.

**5. Skip rules.** If the test allows skipping, I skip any question that looks like 12 s or more, two questions' worth, and return at the end. If it is forward only with +1 and −1, I cannot skip. I remove options fast: a blind guess is worth −0.5, after one removal −1/3, after two 0. So I guess only after removing two, or when unreached questions would score nothing anyway.

**6. The first minute.** I start at a steady 6 s and let any hard early question go. Spending 30 s on question 3 costs four questions at the end. I take one breath between blocks of 20.

**7. A bad start.** If I am 15 s behind at 2:00, that is 2.5 questions. I do not rush the easy kinds, which raises slips. I guess faster on the slow kinds, fractions and long sequences, and keep the rest at pace. A slow block costs a few questions; panic costs more.

**8. The day before.** One warm-up round only, a tested link, a quiet room, pen and paper if allowed, and sleep.

rubric.text: Plans daily warm-up rounds with a logged score and a target, such as the Stage 3 mark of 50.
Chooses drills from an error review, naming the kind, the count of questions and a target pace.
Sits a mock during the week and reviews it: net score, block times, slips, method gaps and time losses.
States the checkpoints: Q20 at 2:00, Q40 at 4:00, Q60 at 6:00.
Gives skip rules for both formats: skip and return where allowed; remove options and guess where not, with the guess values.
Applies the first-minute rule and a breath between blocks.
Says how to recover from a bad start, with a number: guess faster on slow kinds rather than rushing easy ones.
